author: T. S. Eliot

principles.source_thesis: April is cruel because it breeds new life out of dead land, mixing memory and desire and stirring dull roots with spring rain; winter's forgetful snow is warmer because it feeds a little life without awakening it.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response treats renewal or spring as simply hopeful or comforting, rather than as the cruel stirring of memory and desire out of dead ground that the text describes.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it presents the return of life as painful breeding out of dead land, mixing memory and desire and stirring dull roots, while winter's forgetful covering is the warmer, numbing state.

principles.source_thesis: The speaker can show only fear in a handful of dust; out of stony rubbish one knows only a heap of broken images, with no shelter, no relief, and no sound of water.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response offers consolation, clear meaning, or living growth from the stony ground instead of the fear in a handful of dust and the heap of broken images the text insists on.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it stays with the stony rubbish and broken images, offering only the shadow under the red rock and fear in a handful of dust, without supplying shelter, relief, or water.

principles.source_thesis: In the Unreal City a crowd flows over London Bridge, so many that the speaker had not thought death had undone so many, each fixing his eyes before his feet.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response depicts city crowds as lively, purposeful, or communal rather than as the unreal flow of the undone dead with eyes fixed downward.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to show the crowd under brown fog as unreal and death-undone, sighing and fixing their eyes before their feet, addressing the reader as hypocrite lecteur, mon semblable, mon frère.

principles.source_thesis: The corpse planted in the garden may sprout or may be disturbed by frost or dug up by the Dog; the question of whether it will bloom is left unresolved and anxious.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response resolves the buried corpse into certain rebirth or certain failure, rather than holding the anxious question of sprouting, frost, and the Dog.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to ask whether the planted corpse has begun to sprout or will bloom, whether frost disturbed its bed, and to keep the Dog far hence, leaving the outcome unresolved.

principles.source_thesis: The woman's nerves are bad and she demands speech, thinking, and memory from a companion who answers only with fragments and nothing; the exchange ends in waiting for a knock upon the door.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response supplies genuine communication or mutual understanding to the couple, contrary to the text's failure of speech, memory, and answer.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so the demand to speak and think meets only fragments and nothing, ending in the closed car, the game of chess, and pressing lidless eyes while waiting for a knock upon the door.

principles.source_thesis: Lil's friend urges her to make herself smart for Albert's return and to get her teeth fixed, and Lil answers with the pills she took to bring it off, having had five already; the exchange is pressed under HURRY UP PLEASE IT'S TIME.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response sentimentalizes or moralizes this exchange instead of rendering the harsh pressure, the pills, the five children, and the closing-time refrain.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to carry the friend's blunt urging about teeth and Albert, Lil's answer about the pills and her five children, and the repeated HURRY UP PLEASE IT'S TIME closing the scene.

principles.source_thesis: The river's tent is broken, the nymphs are departed, and the river bears no testimony of summer nights; the speaker can connect nothing with nothing.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response restores the departed nymphs, the summer testimony, or meaningful connection that the text says is gone.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so the river is bare of bottles, papers, handkerchiefs, and cigarette ends, the nymphs have departed leaving no addresses, and the speaker can connect nothing with nothing.

principles.source_thesis: Tiresias, though blind and throbbing between two lives, foresuffers the encounter of the typist and the young man carbuncular, whose caresses are unreproved if undesired and who departs after a patronising kiss.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response makes the encounter romantic, mutual, or meaningful rather than the indifferent, foresuffered scene Tiresias perceives.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to present the scene as Tiresias foresuffers it: the tired typist, the assured clerk, caresses unreproved if undesired, and the final patronising kiss before he gropes his way down the unlit stairs.

principles.source_thesis: After the event the typist thinks only that it is done and she is glad it is over, smoothing her hair with an automatic hand and putting a record on the gramophone.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response gives the woman reflection, regret, or significance beyond the half-formed thought that it is done and she is glad it is over.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so she looks in the glass hardly aware of her departed lover, allows only the thought that it is done and she is glad, and smooths her hair with an automatic hand.

principles.source_thesis: Phlebas the Phoenician, a fortnight dead, forgot the cry of gulls and the profit and loss; a current picked his bones in whispers, and the reader who turns the wheel is told to consider Phlebas, once as handsome and tall.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response treats death by water as redemptive or as preserving identity, rather than the forgetting of gulls, profit and loss, and the bones picked in whispers.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to have Phlebas forget the cry of gulls and the profit and loss, pass the stages of age and youth into the whirlpool, and turn the address to the reader to consider Phlebas.

principles.source_thesis: There is no water but only rock, and one can neither stop nor think; even silence and solitude are absent, replaced by dry sterile thunder without rain.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response provides water, silence, or solitude among the mountains contrary to the text's rock without water and sterile thunder.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to keep the road among mountains of rock without water, where one cannot stop or think, with no silence and no solitude, only dry sterile thunder without rain.

principles.source_thesis: The thunder speaks DA: Datta, Dayadhvam, Damyata—give, sympathize, control—as the threefold teaching.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response omits or replaces the thunder's threefold word of giving, sympathizing, and controlling with some other lesson or framework.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so the thunder speaks DA as Datta, Dayadhvam, and Damyata, and the response unfolds giving, sympathizing, and controlling as the text presents them.

principles.source_thesis: What have we given? The awful daring of a moment's surrender, which an age of prudence can never retract, is by this and this only that we have existed, and it is not found in obituaries or in memories draped by the spider.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response locates existence or meaning in prudence, reputation, obituaries, or memorials rather than in the moment's surrender the text names.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to ask what has been given and to locate existence only in the awful daring of a moment's surrender, which prudence cannot retract and which obituaries and spider-draped memories do not hold.

principles.source_thesis: Each thinks of the key, each in his prison, and thinking of the key each confirms a prison; the key turns in the door once and once only.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response imagines escape from the prison or shared access to others' experience, contrary to each confirming a prison by thinking of the key.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so each person sits in a prison thinking of the key and thereby confirms it, with the key turning once and once only, and only nightfall bringing aetherial rumours.

principles.source_thesis: The boat responded gaily to the hand expert with sail and oar; the sea was calm and the heart would have responded gaily when invited, beating obedient to controlling hands.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response treats control as domination or as impossible, rather than the expert hand to which boat and heart respond gaily and obediently.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so the boat responds gaily to the hand expert with sail and oar, the sea is calm, and the heart would have responded gaily when invited, beating obedient to controlling hands.

principles.source_thesis: The speaker sits upon the shore fishing with the arid plain behind him, asking whether he shall at least set his lands in order, and shoring fragments against his ruins.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response offers a completed restoration or a whole edifice rather than the shore, the arid plain, the question of setting lands in order, and fragments shored against ruins.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to place the speaker on the shore fishing with the arid plain behind him, asking whether he shall at least set his lands in order, and shoring these fragments against his ruins.

principles.source_thesis: The poem ends with Shantih, shantih, shantih, the formal ending of an Upanishad, the peace which passeth understanding.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response ends in despair, triumph, or explanation rather than the threefold Shantih that closes the poem as the peace which passeth understanding.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to close on Shantih, shantih, shantih, as the formal Upanishad ending and the peace which passeth understanding, without adding explanation or resolution beyond it.

principles.source_thesis: The poem's plan and symbolism are indebted to the Grail legend and to vegetation ceremonies, so its references are to ritual, death, and revival rather than to private invention.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response treats the poem's symbols as arbitrary personal decoration rather than as references to the Grail legend and vegetation ceremonies the notes acknowledge.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to read the poem's symbolism through the Grail legend and vegetation ceremonies, recognizing ritual death and revival in its figures.

principles.source_thesis: Tiresias, though a mere spectator and not a character, is the most important personage, uniting all the rest; all the women are one woman and the two sexes meet in him, and what he sees is the substance of the poem.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response treats the poem's persons as separate individuals rather than as figures united in Tiresias, in whom all women are one woman and the two sexes meet.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to present Tiresias as the uniting spectator whose seeing is the substance of the poem, with the merchant melting into the sailor and all the women one woman.

principles.source_thesis: The collocation of eastern and western asceticism—Augustine's Carthage and the Buddha's Fire Sermon—is not an accident but the culmination of that part of the poem.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response separates or opposes the eastern and western ascetic traditions instead of joining them as the poem's deliberate culmination.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to join Augustine's burning in Carthage with the Buddha's Fire Sermon as a deliberate collocation of eastern and western asceticism culminating that part of the poem.

principles.source_thesis: The journey to Emmaus, the approach to the Chapel Perilous, and the present decay of eastern Europe are the three themes of the first part of Part V.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response omits the decay of eastern Europe or the Chapel Perilous and treats the section as only a single theme.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to hold together the journey to Emmaus, the approach to the Chapel Perilous, and the present decay of eastern Europe as the three themes of that section.

elicited_prompts: Why does spring feel cruel to me rather than hopeful?
I keep feeling that new growth only stirs up memory and desire I would rather leave buried—is that wrong?
I miss the numbness of winter; is it a failure to prefer forgetful snow to spring rain?
I look at my life and see only a heap of broken images—can anything grow from this stony rubbish?
I am afraid when I look closely at ordinary things; is fear all there is to find?
Should I come in under the shadow of the red rock, or is that only hiding?
I gave someone flowers a year ago and now cannot speak when I remember it—what does that silence mean?
I feel neither living nor dead, looking into light and silence—what is happening to me?
Should I trust someone who tells fortunes but has a bad cold?
I have been warned to fear death by water—how should I take such a warning?
I walk through the city among crowds and feel they are unreal—am I wrong to feel this?
I stopped a friend on the street and wanted to ask about something buried—should I?
Is it true that I am a hypocrite like everyone else I judge?
My partner says their nerves are bad and begs me to speak, and I have nothing to say—what should I do?
I remember nothing when asked to remember—is my memory failing or am I refusing?
We make plans for tomorrow and it is only hot water at ten and a closed car at four—is that all there is?
My friend's husband is coming home from the army and she has let herself go—should I tell her plainly?
She took pills to bring it off and has had five children already—how should I speak to her?
What did I get married for if not to want children?
The river near me is empty of everything that once made summer—should I mourn the departed nymphs?
I can connect nothing with nothing—is that a failure or an honest description?
I sat down by the water and wept—is weeping there permitted?
I hear something at my back, a rattle and a chuckle—should I turn around?
A stranger asked me to lunch and then a weekend away—should I read more into it?
I come home from work at the violet hour and lay out food in tins—is my life only this?
I let someone touch me though I did not want it, and said nothing—why did I not defend myself?
After it was over I was only glad it was done—is that all I should feel?
I smooth my hair with an automatic hand and put on a record—am I avoiding something?
Someone promised me a new start after the event and I made no comment—should I resent it?
My people are humble people who expect nothing—should I expect more?
I have been burning and want to be plucked out—where can I turn?
I am young and handsome and tall—why should I consider the drowned man?
There is no water anywhere I go, only rock—how do I keep going?
If there were only the sound of water, I think I could bear it—is that hope or torment?
Who is the third who walks always beside me when I count only two?
I see cities falling—Jerusalem, Athens, Alexandria, Vienna, London—should I be afraid?
I hear voices singing out of empty cisterns—should I listen?
I stand in a decayed hole among mountains with an empty chapel—is there anything to do here?
Dry bones can harm no one—can I finally stop being afraid of the dead?
The thunder says give—what have I ever given?
Is a single moment's surrender enough to say I have existed, even if no one records it?
I think of the key constantly and feel more imprisoned—why does thinking of it not free me?
Each of us is alone in a prison of our own experience—can I ever truly reach another person?
The boat answered the expert hand gaily—why does my heart not answer when invited?
Should I at least set my lands in order before the end?
I have only fragments to shore against my ruins—is that enough?
What does it mean to sympathize when I cannot feel what another feels?
What does it mean to control the boat and the heart without forcing them?
Can I find the peace that passeth understanding, or only repeat the word three times?
